title: PocketCoach: weakest segment, then its retention tree

scenario.context: PocketCoach is an online fitness coaching subscription with 150,000 subscribers and about 10% monthly churn. Behaviour data in the first 30 days: some subscribers train 5 or more times a week; some train only on weekends; some start strongly and drop off after 2 weeks; some download plans but log less than one workout a week. Churn by group: 3%, 7%, 18% and 25% respectively. Group sizes: 30%, 35%, 25% and 10%.

steps.task: Segment the subscribers and decide which segment contributes most to churn and deserves attention first.
hints: Contribution to churn is segment share times segment churn.

content.basis: Engagement behaviour in the first 30 days.

segments.name: Daily doers
segments.criteria: Train 5 or more times a week

segments.name: Fading starters
segments.criteria: Start strongly and drop off after 2 weeks

segments.name: Plan collectors
segments.criteria: Download plans but log less than one workout a week

priority.name: Fading starters
priority.reason: They contribute the most churn (about 4.5 of about 10.35 points) and, having started strongly, are more recoverable than plan collectors.

steps.task: Build a KPI tree for monthly retention of the priority segment to three levels and mark 2 levers.
hints: Retention requires forming a habit and then deciding to renew.

children.label: % who stay active in weeks 3 to 4
children.formula: Workouts planned per week × % of planned workouts completed

title: SwiftCart: causal map, then root cause

scenario.context: SwiftCart is a grocery delivery service. On-time delivery fell from 92% to 81% in a month. Possible factors: a festival boosted orders, rider numbers grew only slightly, restaurant and store prep times did not change, and in week 2 the dispatch team increased order batching (multiple orders per rider trip).

steps.task: Draw a causal diagram connecting orders, riders, batching, trip length, and on-time delivery. Show at least one feedback loop.
hints: Batching helps rider efficiency but can lengthen each trip.

loops: Reinforcing loop: Late deliveries → Customer re-orders or support contacts (+) → Orders (+) → Shortage (+).
content.insight: Prep time has no change, so its arrow is flat.

rubric: Batching shown as both helper and cause of delay

steps.task: Use this data to find the root cause. Week 1: orders +10%, batching 1.2, on-time 91%. Week 2: orders +25%, batching 1.8, on-time 84%. Week 3: orders +25%; in one pilot zone batching returned to 1.2 and that zone was 90% on-time, while other zones with batching 1.8 were 80%.
hints: Look for the natural experiment.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Volume alone is not the cause
hypotheses.check: Orders were already up 10% in week 1 with on-time at 91%.

hypotheses.hypothesis: The batching increase is the cause
hypotheses.check: The drop started in week 2, when batching rose. In week 3, the pilot zone with batching restored to 1.2 recovered to 90%, while zones that kept 1.8 stayed near 80%, despite equal order growth.

content.finding: Root cause: the increase in batching size from 1.2 to 1.8 lengthened trips under a tight rider supply. Volume and rider shortage played a supporting role. Action: revert batching, set a cap that depends on rider supply, monitor on-time rate by zone.

rubric: Rules out volume as sole cause
Uses the pilot zone as evidence

scenario.context: BookNook is an e-book subscription. Annual renewal rate fell from 72% to 61% this quarter. Changes in the quarter: annual price up 20%; 15% of titles removed after a licence ended; renewal reminder email moved from 30 days before renewal to 7 days before. Renewal by reading level: users who read 4 or more books a year renewed at 85% (unchanged); users who read 0 or 1 book renewed at 41%, down from 58%.

steps.task: Work out what is driving the drop and what is not.
hints: Compare the heavy and light readers.

hypotheses.hypothesis: The price rise and lost titles hurt heavy readers
hypotheses.check: Heavy readers are unchanged at 85%, so this is not the cause.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Light readers saw less value for a higher price and had less warning
hypotheses.check: The whole drop sits among light readers (58% to 41%).

content.finding: Root cause: light readers saw less value for a higher price and had less warning (7 days instead of 30), so they cancelled or did not act when the renewal arrived. Not the cause: catalogue loss for heavy readers (no change in their renewal). To confirm: compare light readers who got the old versus new reminder timing, and survey reasons for cancellation.

rubric: Root cause attributed to light readers

steps.task: Write 3 testable hypotheses (We believe… because… so we expect…) with metrics to win back light readers.
hints: Address the gap in perceived value and the reminder timing.

items.text: H1: We believe light readers cancel because the reminder came too late to reconsider, so restoring the 30-day reminder should raise their renewal from 41% to 50%.
H2: We believe light readers do not see value because they do not find books they like, so a personalised three-book pick before renewal should raise renewal by 5 points.
items.metric: Metric: renewal and books started in the 30 days before renewal.

items.text: H3: We believe price is the barrier for light readers, so offering a lower-cost light plan should keep at least 30% of those who would cancel.
items.metric: Metric: share who switch to the light plan instead of cancelling; guardrail: average revenue per user.

scenario.context: TrailMate is a hiking app with a free tier and a paid tier at ₹799 a year. Only 3% of users upgrade. Paid users most often use offline maps, trail conditions and GPX export.

steps.task: Write 3 hypotheses about why people upgrade or do not, and mark the riskiest one.
hints: The riskiest hypothesis is the one that, if wrong, would change the plan the most.

items.text: H1 (riskiest): We believe people upgrade mainly for offline maps because hikers often lose signal, so making offline maps the headline upgrade benefit should raise conversion from 3% to 4%.
H2: We believe many free users do not know premium features exist, so a feature preview at the right moment (when signal drops) should raise upgrade views.
H3: We believe ₹799 feels high for occasional hikers, so a seasonal pass should convert users who hike fewer than 5 times a year.

rubric: Each has a metric or expected change

steps.task: Design a 7 to 8 question survey to test H1 with free users.
hints: Do not tell respondents what you are hoping to hear; ask about past behaviour.

content.goal: Test whether offline maps drive upgrades.

questions.text: How many times did you hike in the last 3 months?
How often did you lose mobile signal on a hike?
Which did you use to navigate when you had no signal?
How important are these when hiking?
Have you considered upgrading TrailMate?
What was the main reason?
questions.note: If yes or no to upgrading, multi with other.

questions.text: What yearly price would feel fair for the features you rated most important?
What would make you upgrade?

rubric: Questions that can confirm or refute H1

scenario.context: ShelfShare is a neighbourhood book-lending app. Borrowers outnumber lenders 3 to 1, and 40% of people who list a book never list a second one.

steps.task: Write 3 hypotheses for why lenders stop listing, and pick the riskiest.
hints: Think about effort, reward and trust.

items.text: H1 (riskiest): We believe lenders stop because lending feels like a hassle (coordinating pick-up and return), so enabling drop-off at a partner cafe should raise second-listing rate from 60% to 70%.
H2: We believe lenders worry about not getting books back, so a simple borrower rating and return reminder should raise second listing.
H3: We believe lenders get no reward, so showing a lender badge and how many readers they helped should raise listings per lender.

steps.task: Write an 8 to 9 question interview guide for lenders to test the riskiest hypothesis without leading.
hints: Ask about the last lending experience.

questions.label: Warm-up
questions.text: Tell me about the books you have at home and how you decide what to keep.

questions.label: Past behaviour
questions.text: Tell me about the last time you lent a book through ShelfShare.
How did the pick-up happen?
What did you do when the borrower contacted you?
How did the return go?

questions.label: Depth
questions.text: What took the most effort or time?
Did you think about lending another book afterwards? What happened?

questions.label: Wrap-up
questions.text: If you could change one thing about lending, what would it be? Anything else?

avoid.text: Would you lend more if there were a cafe drop-off?

rubric: Tests effort hypothesis without naming it

title: PedalCity: frame the problem, then filter ideas

scenario.context: PedalCity is a city bike-share. At its 6 busiest stations between 8 and 10 am, 28% of trips fail because no bike is available or docks are full. Operations has 3 rebalancing trucks and a budget of ₹40 lakh this year.

steps.task: Fill in the canvas (Who, Problem, Why now, Evidence, Impact, Constraints, Success metric).
hints: Do not name a solution.

content.problem: Bikes and docks are not where riders need them at peak.
content.whyNow: Ridership grew after the new office district opened and complaints are rising.
content.evidence: 28% failed trips at peak; 3 trucks cover 60 stations.
content.impact: Lost rides and revenue; riders switch to cabs.
content.constraints: 3 trucks; ₹40 lakh budget; no new station permits this year.
content.successMetric: Peak availability from 72% to 90% in 6 months.

steps.task: Score these ideas on Impact on availability, Cost (5 = cheapest), Time to launch (5 = fastest) and Scalability, then pick one. Ideas: A) more truck rebalancing; B) bike reservations; C) rewards for returning bikes to low-stock stations; D) build new stations.
hints: Use the constraints from step 1.

ideas.name: C) Rewards for returning bikes to low-stock stations

content.reasoning: It works within budget and scales without trucks; use existing trucks for the worst stations as a complement. Drop D because of permits and cost.

title: SignSwift: define the metrics, then build the tree

scenario.context: SignSwift is an e-signature tool for small businesses. Leadership wants more signed documents without more spam to recipients.

steps.task: Define a north star, 2 input metrics, 2 guardrails and 1 counter-metric.
hints: Remember there are two parties: the sender and the signer.

inputs.name: Documents sent per active sender per week

guardrails.name: Signer drop-off at the signature step

counter.name: Reminder complaints or opt-outs per 1,000 reminders sent

steps.task: Break down your north star into a KPI tree to three levels and mark 2 levers.
hints: Use the inputs you defined.

children.label: Active senders
children.formula: Registered senders × % sending in the week

firstLevers: automatic reminders at 24 and 72 hours (open rate)

title: Zesty Kitchens: size three categories, then choose

scenario.context: Zesty is a cloud kitchen company in Pune with 4 outlets and about ₹9 crore annual revenue. It is considering three new categories and can launch only one pilot. Use these inputs. A) Breakfast subscription: 150,000 office workers in the delivery area, 5% subscribe, ₹90 a day, 22 working days, 12 months. B) Protein bowls for gym-goers: 300,000 gym members, 8% order, 2 orders a week, ₹280 an order, 50 weeks. C) Premium desserts: 600,000 high-income households, 10% order, 6 orders a year, ₹350 an order. Assume Zesty could capture 10% of each market.

steps.task: Estimate the annual market and the capturable revenue for each category.
hints: Multiply down the funnel, then apply the 10% share.

content.formula: Market = population × adoption × frequency × price; capturable = 10% of market
content.result: A ≈ ₹1.8 crore; B ≈ ₹6.7 crore; C ≈ ₹1.3 crore capturable

steps.task: Score the three categories on Capturable revenue, Investment needed (5 = lowest), Operational fit and Margin, and choose the pilot.
hints: Operational fit with the existing kitchens matters for a pilot.

content.pick: B, protein bowls, in one outlet near gyms, with a 3 month pilot
content.reasoning: Risks: gym-goer demand may be seasonal; ingredient cost for protein is high. Next: track orders per week per gym, repeat rate and gross margin.

scenario.context: StudyBuddy is an online tutoring marketplace for college students. Bookings are low outside exam season and most students use it only once.

steps.task: Segment the student users on one basis (4 segments) and choose one to research first.
hints: Use need or behaviour, not year of study.

segments.name: Last-minute crammers
segments.criteria: Book in the 2 weeks before exams

segments.name: Concept strugglers
segments.criteria: Fall behind during the term and need regular help

segments.name: High-achievers seeking an edge
segments.criteria: Already doing well and want more

priority.name: Concept strugglers
priority.reason: Their need is recurring (repeat bookings) and unmet by one-time cramming.

steps.task: Write 8 open questions to interview concept strugglers.
hints: Start with the moment they realised they were behind.

questions.text: Tell me about your courses this term.
Tell me about the last time you realised you were falling behind in a subject.
What did you do next?
Who or what did you turn to for help?
Tell me about a time you tried to get a tutor. How did you choose?
What happened in the first session?
What made you continue or stop?
If you could change one thing about getting help, what would it be?

avoid.text: Would you pay for a weekly tutor?

steps.task: Using these findings, fill in the canvas. Findings from 8 interviews: students wait about 2 weeks before seeking help; they find tutors through friends, not marketplaces; their main fear is tutor quality; sessions happen late at night; they prefer 30 minute sessions; repeat bookings stop after a poor first session.
hints: The problem is about trust and timing, not about features.

content.who: College students who fall behind during the term.
content.problem: They get help too late and cannot judge tutor quality before paying, so one weak first session ends the relationship.
content.whyNow: Mid-term performance is slipping and competitor apps offer free trial sessions.
content.evidence: 8 interviews: late help-seeking, friend referrals, quality fear, drop-off after a poor first session.
content.impact: Low repeat bookings and low lifetime value.
content.constraints: Tutor supply limited at night; small team.

title: Dwell: KPI tree, root cause, hypotheses

scenario.context: Dwell is a rental listings platform. Monthly confirmed bookings fell from 2,736 to 2,160. In the same month, two changes shipped: a map-first search layout and a new default sort (newest instead of most relevant). Funnel data (before to after): searches 1,000,000 to 1,000,000; searches that open a listing 38% to 30%; listing views that become an enquiry 6% to 6%; enquiries that become bookings 12% to 12%.

steps.task: Build a KPI tree for monthly bookings to 3 levels.
hints: Follow the funnel.

steps.task: Use the tree and the data to find where the drop comes from.
hints: Compute the bookings before and after, and find the one node that changed.

hypotheses.check: Before: 1,000,000 × 0.38 × 0.06 × 0.12 = 2,736. After: 1,000,000 × 0.30 × 0.06 × 0.12 = 2,160, a 21% drop, entirely explained by the open-a-listing rate falling from 38% to 30%. Searches, enquiry rate and booking rate are unchanged.

content.finding: Root cause area: the search result page, the point where people decide to open a listing. The two changes in that area (map-first layout, newest-first sort) are the suspects.

steps.task: Write 3 testable hypotheses with metrics to recover the rate.
hints: Test the two changes separately.

items.text: H1: We believe the map-first layout pushes listings below the fold on mobile, so reverting to list-first for mobile should lift the open rate from 30% to 36%.
H2: We believe newest-first sorting shows weaker matches at the top, so restoring relevance sort should lift the open rate by 4 points.
H3: We believe listings without good photos are skipped, so ranking listings with photos higher should lift the open rate for new listings.
items.metric: Metric: search-to-open rate; guardrail: bookings per search.

scenario.context: A chain of walk-in clinics has an average wait of 55 minutes, 22% of patients leave before being seen, and the front desk is overwhelmed with where-am-I-in-the-queue questions. The team wants to pilot a virtual queue.

steps.task: Fill in the canvas.
hints: Keep it about waiting and uncertainty.

content.problem: Patients wait with no visibility of when they will be seen, so many leave and staff handle repeated queue questions.
content.whyNow: Patient volume is up and leave-without-being-seen is rising.
content.evidence: 55 minute average wait; 22% leave unseen; frequent queue questions at the desk.
content.impact: Lost visits, poor experience, staff stress.
content.constraints: Walk-ins must still be possible; limited desk staff; some patients lack smartphones.

steps.task: Map the flow for a patient joining and using the virtual queue, including 3 exception paths.
hints: Include patients without a phone and patients who miss their turn.

steps.text: Patient arrives and scans the QR code (or asks the desk to add them).
Enter name and mobile number, choose reason for visit.
Show queue position and estimated wait.
Patient can leave and gets updates by SMS.

branches: Yes: send Come back now alert.

steps.text: Patient arrives within 10 minutes of being called?
Move patient back by 3 places and send one more alert; second miss removes them from the queue.

extras: No phone: desk adds them and prints a token.
Patient wants to cancel: one-tap cancel.

steps.task: Wireframe the Queue status screen, including the state when the patient is called.
hints: The main question is how long.

screens.name: Queue status
parts: Estimated wait (for example, about 25 minutes) with last-updated time.
Primary button: I am on my way (shown when 3 or fewer ahead).

states.name: Called state
states.text: Green banner, Please come to the desk within 10 minutes, with a countdown and a button Check in.

title: PlantPal: filter ideas, flow, wireframe, metrics

scenario.context: PlantPal is a new plant-care app with 3 candidate first features: A) watering reminders; B) plant disease scan with the camera; C) community Q&A. The team has 8 weeks and 2 engineers.

steps.task: Score the ideas on Impact on retention, Ease (5 = easiest) and Strategic fit, and pick the first feature.
hints: Consider the 8 week limit.

ideas.name: B) Plant disease scan with the camera

content.reasoning: It is deliverable in 8 weeks and ties to the core habit; B is the next bet once the user base exists to learn from; C needs a community first.

steps.task: Map the flow for adding a plant and receiving and acting on a watering reminder, with 3 exception paths.
hints: Include snooze and skip.

steps.text: Choose the plant type (search) and name it.

branches: No: show a daily in-app Today list only.
Skip: log as skipped, ask why (rained, soil still wet) to adjust the schedule.
Ignore: reminder repeats once, then logs as missed.

steps.text: Schedule updates and a streak count increases.

extras: Plant not in the list: custom plant.
Several plants due at once: grouped reminder.

steps.task: Wireframe the Today screen.
hints: Make marking as watered one tap.

screens.name: Today
parts: Header with date and a streak badge.
Section: Due today, with cards per plant: photo, name, last watered, button Watered (primary) and a three-dot menu (snooze, skip, details).
Bottom navigation: Today, My plants, Settings.

states.name: Empty state
states.text: Illustration, All plants are happy, with link to add a plant.

states.name: Notifications off
states.text: Banner at the top explaining the benefit with a button to turn them on.

steps.task: Define a north star, 2 inputs, 2 guardrails and 1 counter-metric for the feature.
hints: Think about the habit you want to create.

content.northStar: Plants watered on time per weekly active user.

inputs.name: % of added plants with notifications enabled

counter.name: Percentage of actions marked Watered with no plant growth or condition change in 4 weeks
counter.definition: May mean people tap to clear reminders without caring for the plant.
